title: pyarrow.lib.ArrowTypeError:  "Expected a string or bytes object, got a 'int' object"
description:
could in-place type coercion or promotion be applied with a warning to prevent this?

```py
import pandas as pd

testdf = pd.DataFrame({'testcol':['item1', 'item2', 3, 'item4']})

testdf.to_feather('testdf.feather')

```

end of Traceback
```py
 File "pyarrow/array.pxi", line 182, in pyarrow.lib.array
 File "pyarrow/array.pxi", line 82, in pyarrow.lib._ndarray_to_array
 File "pyarrow/error.pxi", line 91, in pyarrow.lib.check_status
pyarrow.lib.ArrowTypeError: ("Expected a string or bytes object, got a 'int' object", 'Conversion failed for column testcol with type object')

```


Simple work-around:

```py
import pandas as pd

testdf = pd.DataFrame({'testcol':['item1', 'item2', 3, 'item4']})
testdf['testcol'] = testdf['testcol'].astype(str)

testdf.to_feather('testdf.feather')
```

title: Feature request: Read and write dataset description in both R and Python
description:
The R-help for `feather_metadata` states: "Returns the dimensions, field names, and types; and optional dataset description.". @hrbrmstr Kindly posted a [PR](https://github.com/wesm/feather/pull/326) to make this feature work and read and write a dataset description to a feather file from R. The dataset description could contain variable definitions, data source, etc., perhaps in markdown format.

It would be great if it were possible to read (and write) such a dataset description in python / pandas using feather.read_dataframe and feather.write_dataframe as well. I searched the documentation but couldn't find any information about this. It was hoping something like the following might work:

import feather
import pandas as pd
dat = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2, 3], 'b': [4, 5, 6]})
dat._metadata = "# Test dataset\n\nThis dataset contains information on ..."
feather.write_dataframe(dat, "pydf.feather")

Or else perhaps:

feather.write_dataframe(dat, "pydf.feather", "# Test dataset\n\nThis dataset contains information on ...")

See also this [post on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47917549/read-and-write-a-dataset-description-as-a-pandas-dataframe-attribute)

title: is the format stable?
description:
My impression from taking to @wesm before was that it wasn't yet, and that you still reserved the right to make breaking changes (esp. since the format isn't even documented outside of the source code, never mind having been peer reviewed). But it looks like people are using it now, and there doesn't seem to be any statement either way anywhere public that I can find.

It would be good to add a prominent notice to the readme describing what the current stability (non-)guarantees actually are.

title: Index lost during pandas-feather-pandas roundtrip
description:
When persisting a pandas DataFrame to feather, the row index seems to get lost. When pulling the frame out again, the index is replaced with a RangeIndex. The column index remains intact.

This [example notebook](https://gist.github.com/aleyan/76b230f3f1eca4de500107f6e6e53caf) illustrates the issue.

Not sure if this is a design decision or a bug or something else. My use case for feather is to roundtrip data through the filesystem with greater confidence that it won't get mangled like in CSVs. For now my work around is to reset_index() before saving and then do set_index() after loading.

title: python feather-format 0.4.0 is incompatible with pyarrow 0.17.0: ImportError FeatherError FeatherReader FeatherWriter
description:
Installed `feather-format` and `pyarrow` in python 3.8.2 today, ran into this problem resulting in an `ImportError`.

The `feather` script `api.py` tries to import:

```python
from pyarrow.feather import (read_feather as read_dataframe,  # noqa
                             write_feather as write_dataframe,
                             FeatherError,
                             FeatherReader,
                             FeatherWriter)
```
But in pyarrow 0.17.0, `FeatherError` and `FeatherReader` have moved to `pyarrow.lib`. I don't know where `FeatherWriter` went, I couldn't find it.

So, I uninstalled `pyarrow` and `python -m pip install pyarrow==0.16.0` instead, fixed the problem.

Just a heads up that people will start running into this problem.

title: [R] Encoding info losses for non-ASCII column names
description:
If the column names contain non-ASCII strings, the `Encoding` info will be lost when reading from the local feather file. The following example is run on my Mac. 

It will be even worse if it's run on a Windows machine because it seems like `feather` will try to convert the column names to `native` encoding from `unknown` encoding, leading to garbage column names that can never be converted back.

### Minimal Reproducible Example

```r
utf8_strings <- c("çile", "façile", "El. paÅ¡tas", "¡tas", "Þ")
latin1_strings <- iconv(utf8_strings, from = "UTF-8", to = "latin1")
tbl <- data.frame(utf8_strings, latin1_strings, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
colnames(tbl) <- c(utf8_strings[2], latin1_strings[2])
tbl2 <- local({
  tmp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".feather")
  on.exit(unlink(tmp_file), add = TRUE)
  feather::write_feather(tbl, tmp_file)
  feather::read_feather(tmp_file)
})
colnames(tbl)
#> [1] "façile" "façile"
colnames(tbl2)
#> [1] "façile"    "fa\xe7ile" ############SEE HERE############
Encoding(colnames(tbl))
#> [1] "UTF-8"  "latin1"
Encoding(colnames(tbl2))
#> [1] "unknown" "unknown"
Encoding(colnames(tbl2)) <- c("UTF-8", "latin1")
colnames(tbl2)
#> [1] "façile" "façile"
```

title: Timestamp, Time, Date, and Category types values aren't written to disk
description:
In my efforts to create a [.NET implementation of a Feather reader/writer](https://github.com/kevin-montrose/FeatherDotNet), I discovered that some column type values are never written to disk.

In particular

 - [CATEGORY](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/cpp/src/feather/metadata.fbs#L23) is serialized as an INT32
 - [DATE](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/cpp/src/feather/metadata.fbs#L26) also as an INT32
 - [TIMESTAMP](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/cpp/src/feather/metadata.fbs#L25) as an INT64
 - [TIME](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/cpp/src/feather/metadata.fbs#L27)  also as an INT64

In each case the "actual" type can be distinguished based on the column's associated metadata.

Is this behavior intended?  If so, it would probably make sense to remove CATEGORY, DATE, TIMESTAMP, and TIME from the [list of Types](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/master/cpp/src/arrow/ipc/feather.fbs#L27) and document their expected underlying types (or are they allowed to vary?).

title: Slightly confusing error messages with unsupported data?
description:
Say you run

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import feather

df = pd.DataFrame({'nope': np.array([2.0, 3.5], dtype=np.float16)})
feather.write_dataframe(df, 'test.feather')
```

this raises `FeatherError: Invalid: unsupported type 23` ( The corresponding error for the same offense in the `julia` wrapper is `LoadError: KeyError: key Float16 not found`)


if you run 

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({'nope': np.array([np.nan, np.nan], dtype=np.object)})
feather.write_dataframe(df, 'test.feather')
```

you get `ValueError: cannot serialize column 0 named nope with dtype floating`. (in `julia`: `LoadError: argument is an abstract type; size is indeterminate`)

In the first case, I would be at fault for not realising that the [list of supported column types](https://github.com/wesm/feather) does not include `Float16`. The second case is very contrived, but happened to pop up when I foolishly tried to convert a messy CSV to feather without cleaning it first, and at first glance that column looked like a float. 

My point was just if you get error messages like these on a large dataframes, it can be hard to pinpoint the offending column and what the problem is. In the python wrapper [check_status](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/python/feather/ext.pyx#L52) could maybe print the offending column name? (Perhaps the different wrappers could harmonize the error messages?)  Sorry if this is just me being slow (please close this issue if so).

title: Fall-back type (string) for un-supported feather data type.
description:
As reported by other users (e.g, #121, #174), feather can fail to handle unrecognized data types. Because it is not always possible to find equivalent datatypes between R and Python, this error will persist, and prevent data communication between Python and R, even if only one irrelevant column is causing the problem.

I therefore propose that, instead of raising an exception, feather would create a column with string representation of the data. A warning message could be given but the majority of the data would still be passed, and the column with unknown type can most-likely still be handled with some post-processing.

title: Allow saving to compressed files
description:

I work a lot with files stored on an NFS network drive, and `feather.write_dataframe` stresses our network and creates files which are much larger than the equivalent gzip-compressed CSVs. I tried running `gzip -9` on a feather file and got ~10x reduction in size.

I know compression has been mentioned already (#24, #76), but those seem to deal with changing the feather format to support block compression. I just want to gzip the entire file *at the same time* as I am saving it (and not afterwards using `gzip`).

Thank you!

title: feather doesn't play well with simuPOP
description:
Hello, 

This might be a non-issue, but I wanted to bring it to your attention in the case there are other conflicts.

I found out that I had [an issue](https://github.com/BoPeng/simuPOP/issues/3) with import order of feather ([here's a working example](https://github.com/zkamvar/simupop-example)) and another module called [simuPOP](https://github.com/BoPeng/simuPOP/). This was only an issue on Ubuntu (14.04 and 16.04), it worked fine on OSX.

If feather was imported before simuPOP, an error from simuPOP was raised. [When feather was imported after simuPOP, it was no issue](https://github.com/BoPeng/simuPOP/issues/3#issuecomment-243834067).

Here's a MWE with conda:

``` sh
conda update --all 
conda install python=3.4 
conda install -c https://conda.binstar.org/bpeng simuPOP
conda install numpy
pip install feather-format

git clone https://github.com/zkamvar/simupop-example
cd simupop-example/testpopp

# fails
python -c 'import feather;from simuPOP import *;loadPopulation("seed_0_sex_0.0000_gen_00000_rep_00.pop")'

# works
python -c 'from simuPOP import *;import feather;loadPopulation("seed_0_sex_0.0000_gen_00000_rep_00.pop")'
```

Again, I don't know if this is relevant at all, but I just wanted to bring it to your attention.

description:
I noticed odd behavior when writing/reading a dataframe that contained columns with data of mixed-types. Instead of throwing an error or showing a warning, feather silently drops the second data type it encounters.

Instead, it would be helpful if feather stopped processing the file or at least printed a warning instead of silently dropping data. Here's a sample script to demonstrate the behavior:

```
# feather version: 0.2.0

import feather
import pandas

rec_1 = {'a': '1', 'b': '2'}

df1 = pd.DataFrame([rec_1, rec_2])
```

title: Memory => File Layout Compatibility between Feather and Arrow
description:
Do forgive if this isn't the right forum (I also considered the Arrow mailing list, but this seemed more appropriate given the question around feather).

In one of @wesm recent talks (at PyData Berlin I think?), one issue he mentioned was the current inefficiency of having to convert between the feather file format and the internal R/pandas dataframe representation (see [this slide](http://www.slideshare.net/wesm/python-data-ecosystem-thoughts-on-building-for-the-future/32?src=clipshare)), with a seeming assumption that it would be more efficient if you could read a feather file directly into an in-memory Arrow structure. (and then have data processing abilities on that structure, such as provided by pandas/dplyr/etc).

After digging into both feather & Arrow, I've been contemplating having a setup in Julia where we not only leverage @dmbates [beginning work](https://github.com/JuliaStats/Feather.jl) on reading feather files, but also having a corresponding Julia structure following the Arrow memory layout specifications. (perhaps eventually replacing the internal representation of Julia's DataFrame itself, see extensive discussion on DataFrames.jl "soul" [here](https://github.com/JuliaStats/DataFrames.jl/issues/744)).

My main questions at this point are:
- Does this seem like an over-arching good/bad idea?
- Are the feather file format and Arrow memory layouts expected to be synchronous over the long-term?

As a specific question related to the second point, the feather format currently includes the layout of a primitive array like:

```
<null bitmask, optional> <values>
```

whereas Arrow specifies:

```
* Length: 5, Null count: 1
* Null bitmap buffer:

  |Byte 0 (validity bitmap) | Bytes 1-63            |
  |-------------------------|-----------------------|
  |00011011                 | 0 (padding)           |

* Value Buffer:

  |Bytes 0-3   | Bytes 4-7   | Bytes 8-11  | Bytes 12-15 | Bytes 16-19 | Bytes 20-63 |
  |------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
  | 1          | 2           | unspecified | 4           | 8           | unspecified |
```

The difference being Arrow seems to require the length and null_count to be laid out before the null bitmask and values array, whereas these are stored in the "metadata" section of a feather file for each column.

I'm just wondering if little differences in layout like these are to be expected going forward where it makes sense or if there will be efforts to match the layouts more exactly.

title: [feature request] support for non UTF-8 encoded Unicode strings
description:
In issue #74, it was brought up than only UTF-8 encoding for strings was supported by the feather format.
I believe that that can be rather limiting: https://github.com/wesm/feather/issues/74#issuecomment-217234474, since that doesn't work well with a number of languages that either use UTF-16, or support multiple internal representations (such as Python in 3.3 or later), Swift, or Julia.

Some parameters (like "[${BUILD_SUPPORT_DIR}/cpplint.py](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/ecf4f87a51688103b256b571146166daf02131ac/cpp/CMakeLists.txt#L173)" and "[${OUTPUT_DIR}](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/1c09667f131ebe8667b64884fcc3dbf366af7a99/cpp/src/feather/CMakeLists.txt#L75)") are passed to CMake commands in your build scripts without enclosing them by quotation marks. title: [feature request] support for user-level metadata
description:
Idea would be to allow a restricted metadata to be attached globally? per-column? of types that are serializable by `feather`. something like. The usecase I am thinking is to allow pandas to support complete round-tripping.

e.g.

```
In [3]: df = pd.DataFrame({'A' : ['foo','foo','bar'], 'B' : [1,2,3]})

In [4]: df
Out[4]: 
     A  B
0  foo  1
1  foo  2
2  bar  3

In [5]: feather.write_dataframe(df, 'foo.fth')

In [6]: feather.read_dataframe('foo.fth')
Out[6]: 
     A  B
0  foo  1
1  foo  2
2  bar  3

In [7]: feather.read_dataframe('foo.fth').equals(df)
Out[7]: True

In [8]: sdf = df.set_index('A')

In [9]: sdf
Out[9]: 
     B
A     
foo  1
foo  2
bar  3

In [10]: feather.write_dataframe(sdf, 'foo.fth')

In [11]: feather.read_dataframe('foo.fth')
Out[11]: 
   B
0  1
1  2
2  3
```

so on [11] loosing the 'metadata'. But in a pandas wrapper if I could do:

```
feather.write_data_frame(sdf.reset_index(), 'foo.fth', {'index' : ['A']})

df, metadata = feather.read_frame('foo.fth', return_metadata=True)
df = df.set_index(metadata['index'])
```

Then I could round-trip exactly.

HDF5 allows support for _arbitrary_ metadata on the group nodes (it just pickles this). But I think that would be out-of-scope here as its not cross-lang compat.

I think this would nicely solve the representation problem (everything still stored as table likes), but the metadata can offer an alternative interpretation w/o getting in the way of others.

title: perf: interesting results
description:
pandas 0.18.0 / feather a58e3bef81c810091a081eb899961a7475b62dfc

mixed types

```
In [1]: df = pd.DataFrame({'A' : np.random.randn(1000000)})

In [2]: df['B'] = 'foo'

In [3]: df['C'] = pd.Timestamp('20130101')

In [4]: %timeit df.to_hdf('foo.h5', 'df')
1 loop, best of 3: 803 ms per loop

In [5]: %timeit pd.read_hdf('foo.h5', 'df')
1 loop, best of 3: 319 ms per loop

In [6]: import feather

In [7]: %timeit feather.write_dataframe(df, 'foo.fth')
10 loops, best of 3: 62.2 ms per loop

In [8]: %timeit feather.read_dataframe('foo.fth')
10 loops, best of 3: 56.8 ms per loop

In [9]: !ls -ltr foo*
-rw-rw-r--  1 jreback  staff  72487885 Mar 29 23:49 foo.h5
-rw-rw-r--  1 jreback  staff  23000356 Mar 29 23:50 foo.fth

In [10]: %timeit df.to_msgpack('foo.pak')
10 loops, best of 3: 160 ms per loop

In [12]: %timeit pd.read_msgpack('foo.pak')
10 loops, best of 3: 79.8 ms per loop

In [13]: %timeit df.to_msgpack('foo.pak', compress='blosc')
10 loops, best of 3: 139 ms per loop

In [14]: %timeit pd.read_msgpack('foo.pak')
10 loops, best of 3: 72 ms per loop
```

Just floats

```
In [20]: %timeit feather.write_dataframe(df[['A']], 'foo.fth')
100 loops, best of 3: 14.8 ms per loop

In [21]: %timeit feather.read_dataframe('foo.fth')
100 loops, best of 3: 7.47 ms per loop

In [22]: %timeit df[['A']].to_hdf('foo.h5', 'df')
10 loops, best of 3: 34 ms per loop

In [23]: %timeit pd.read_hdf('foo.h5', 'df')
100 loops, best of 3: 9.17 ms per loop

In [24]: %timeit df[['A']].to_msgpack('foo.pak', compress='blosc')
10 loops, best of 3: 37.3 ms per loop

In [25]: %timeit pd.read_msgpack('foo.pak')
100 loops, best of 3: 9.39 ms per loop

In [29]: !ls -ltr foo*
-rw-rw-r--  1 jreback  staff   8000152 Mar 29 23:55 foo.fth
-rw-rw-r--  1 jreback  staff  64487821 Mar 29 23:55 foo.h5
-rw-rw-r--  1 jreback  staff   8000310 Mar 30 00:00 foo.pak
```

Just some ad-hoc perf tests. floats about similar (but better than HDF5, slightly better than msgpack). 
Interesting that feather is WAY faster on fixed length strings in HDF5. (Almost about 1/3 serialized size, which obviously makes writing faster). Note these are the same length strings.

These are _slightly_ non-comparable, as the pandas routines are serializeing the index as well (so doing 2x the work for floats and 1 1/3 more for HDF5/msgpack).

title: iterate over columns directly
description:
https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/python/feather/api.py#L29

you can do something like:

```
def write_dataframe(df, path):
    '''
    Write a pandas.DataFrame to Feather format
    '''
    writer = ext.FeatherWriter(path)

    for i, (name, col) in enumerate(df.iteritems()):

        if not isinstance(name, six.string_types):
            name = str(name)

        writer.write_array(name, col)

    writer.close()
```

handles duplicated names & (non-duplicated), should have better perf that the existing.

title: In R, Feather cannot read dataframe back if missing or having empty column header
description:
In R, when calling `read_feather` function to load the cache, it could fail with error to ask to name columns, if the original dataframe is missing one, which is quite common for datasets (e.g. no index/rownames header). 

The error seems to do with the `tibble` package in the implementation.

If the column name is required, `write_feather` should ask for it if missing in the first place; or the implementation should allow missing columns.

Code example to show the bug is as below:
```r
> library(feather) 
> n = c(2, 3, 5) 
> s = c("aa", "bb", "cc") 
> b = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) 
> df = data.frame(n, s, b)
> df
  n  s     b
1 2 aa  TRUE
2 3 bb FALSE
3 5 cc  TRUE
> colnames(df)[1] <- ""
> df
     s     b
1 2 aa  TRUE
2 3 bb FALSE
3 5 cc  TRUE
> write_feather(df, '~/cache/test.feather')

Error: Column 1 must be named.
Use .name_repair to specify repair.
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

title: Should feather::read_feather respect options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)?
description:

Is there any reason why the R implementation of `read_feather()` ignores the state of the `stringsAsFactors` option?

For consistency, it seems like it would be useful to have it behave in a similar manner to `read.delim()`, `read_tsv()`, etc...

Ex:

```r
library(feather)
library(tidyverse)
options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

write_tsv(head(iris), 'test.tsv')
write_feather(head(iris), 'test.feather')

head(read.delim('test.tsv', sep='\t')$Species)
# [1] "setosa" "setosa" "setosa" "setosa" "setosa" "setosa"

head(read_tsv('test.tsv', col_types = cols())$Species)
# [1] "setosa" "setosa" "setosa" "setosa" "setosa" "setosa"

# [1] setosa setosa setosa setosa setosa setosa
```

Has this happened to others?  Is there a fix for it?

title: question: sparse support / plans?
description:
Hey.
So openml.org is looking (aka I'm trying to convince them) to move away from ARFF as the primary storage format.
I'm trying to understand the scope of feather better to see if it's a candidate.
Sorry if this has been answered elsewhere, I'm not trying to revive #188.

I saw that sparse dataframes are supported but I didn't find a lot of details. I assume because it's a columnar format there is some overhead involved for each column?

And interesting use-case is text data in bag-of-words format which is usually hundreds of thousands of features/columns. Would that be feasible or would you say that's out of scope / not a good fit?

Using feature-hashing can go even more extreme where there might be tens of millions of columns, some of them potentially completely empty.

Thanks!

title: crazy timestamp bug in feather?
description:
Hello the dream team,

Thanks for this wonderful package. I was playing with feather and some timestamps and I noticed some dangerous behavior. Maybe it is a bug. 

Consider this

```
import pandas as pd
import feather
import numpy as np


df = pd.DataFrame({'string_time_utc' : [pd.to_datetime('2018-02-01 14:00:00.531'), 
                                  pd.to_datetime('2018-02-01 14:01:00.456'),
                                  pd.to_datetime('2018-03-05 14:01:02.200')]})

df['timestamp_est'] = pd.to_datetime(df.string_time_utc).dt.tz_localize('UTC').dt.tz_convert('US/Eastern').dt.tz_localize(None)

df
Out[17]: 
          string_time_utc           timestamp_est
0 2018-02-01 14:00:00.531 2018-02-01 09:00:00.531
1 2018-02-01 14:01:00.456 2018-02-01 09:01:00.456
2 2018-03-05 14:01:02.200 2018-03-05 09:01:02.200
```
Here I create the corresponding `EST` timestamp of my original timestamps (in `UTC` time).

Now saving the dataframe to `csv` or to `feather` will generate two completely different results.

```
df.to_csv('P://testing.csv')
df.to_feather('P://testing.feather')
```
Switching to R. 

Using the good old `csv` gives me something a bit annoying, but expected. R thinks my timezone is `UTC` by default, and wrongly attached this timezone to `timestamp_est`. No big deal, I can always use `with_tz` or even better: import as character and process as timestamp while in R.

```
> dataframe <- read_csv('P://testing.csv')
Parsed with column specification:
cols(
  X1 = col_integer(),
  string_time_utc = col_datetime(format = ""),
  timestamp_est = col_datetime(format = "")
)
Warning message:
Missing column names filled in: 'X1' [1] 
> 
> dataframe %>% mutate(mytimezone = tz(timestamp_est))
# A tibble: 3 x 4
     X1 string_time_utc         timestamp_est          
  <int> <dttm>                  <dttm>                 
1     0 2018-02-01 14:00:00.530 2018-02-01 09:00:00.530
2     1 2018-02-01 14:01:00.456 2018-02-01 09:01:00.456
3     2 2018-03-05 14:01:02.200 2018-03-05 09:01:02.200
  mytimezone
  <chr>     
1 UTC       
2 UTC       
3 UTC 
```
Now look at what happens with `feather`:

```
> dataframe <- read_feather('P://testing.feather')
> 
> dataframe %>% mutate(mytimezone = tz(timestamp_est))
# A tibble: 3 x 3
  string_time_utc         timestamp_est           mytimezone
  <dttm>                  <dttm>                  <chr>     
1 2018-02-01 09:00:00.531 2018-02-01 04:00:00.531 ""        
2 2018-02-01 09:01:00.456 2018-02-01 04:01:00.456 ""        
3 2018-03-05 09:01:02.200 2018-03-05 04:01:02.200 ""     
```
My timestamps have been converted!!! pure insanity. 
Am I missing something here?

Thanks!!

title: subset behaves strangely with feather
description:
Hello,

I don't know if the 'subset' function is supposed to work or not on feather files opened with the function 'feather' but I get different behaviours that are not very explicit. It looks like some method is inconstently implemented.

Example 1 (original is a data frame):
  data(iris)
  write_feather(iris,"U:/R/iris.feather")
  f<-feather("U:/R/iris.feather")
  subset(f,Species=="setosa")
results  in: 
Error in subset.default(f, Species == "setosa") : 
  objet 'Species' introuvable

Example 2 (original is a tibble):
  b<-read_sas("U:/R/bsa2003.sas7bdat")
  write_feather(b,"U:/R/bsa2003.feather")
  f<-feather("U:/R/bsa2003.feather")
  subset(f,DEP=="86")
succeeds, but selects only one column (the DEP column), while a subset on the original 'b' returns the whole 28 columns of the data set.

Best regards
Jean-Luc LIPATZ

title: Feather doesn't preserve datetime.date type when reading a dataframe
description:
My goal is to keep just the date portion of the datetime object in the 'date' column. Here's an example

```python
import pandas as pd
import feather

data = {'date': ['2014-05-01 18:47:05.069722', '2014-05-01 18:47:05.119994', 
                 '2014-05-02 18:47:05.178768', '2014-05-02 18:47:05.230071', 
                 '2014-05-02 18:47:05.230071', '2014-05-02 18:47:05.280592']}
df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns = ['date'])

df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date']).dt.date
print(type(df['date'].iloc[1]))
>>> datetime.date
```
However, when I feather save this data frame and, subsequently, load it, the 'date' column turns into a Panda's timestamp type.

```python
df.to_feather('df')
df = feather.read_dataframe('df')
print(type(df['date'].iloc[1]))
>>> pandas._libs.tslibs.timestamps.Timestamp
```
I now have more information than I'd like since the timestamp includes time information, which I do not need. 

Is this an expected behaviour?

title: IO error reading multiple Feather files in R
description:
I have 18,500 Feather files (all with the same columns and column types) which I want to read in. So I do this:

```
library(feather)
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

paths <- Sys.glob("/media/lmullen/data/chronicling-america/out/*.feather")

read_df <- failwith(NA, function(x) {
  message(x)
  read_feather(x)
})

raw_l <- paths %>% map(read_df)
names(raw_l) <- paths
```

When I run that code, some number of the Feather files (it varies from about 150 to 1500) fail to load with this error. 

```
/media/lmullen/data/chronicling-america/out/sn85042907-1919.feather
Error : IO error: Unable to open file
```

There is nothing actually wrong with those Feather files though. I can `read_feather(path_to_problem_file)` and get back a data frame as expected. I can also get the paths which failed to load, then run `map(paths_that_didnt_load, read_feather)` and load all of them fine.

title: Read multiple feathers into a single tibble
description:
There are many applications where people break up data into several medium-sized objects. It would be great to be able to read multiple feathers into a single tibble object without an intermediate step.

In the below, the memory used is double what should be necessary:
```
library(feather)
library(tidyverse)
iris_big <- bind_rows(lapply(1:10000, function(x) iris)) %>% 
  as_tibble()
pryr::object_size(iris_big)
write_feather(iris_big, "tmp1.feather")
write_feather(iris_big, "tmp2.feather")
pryr::mem_change({
  featherdf1 <- read_feather("tmp1.feather")
  featherdf2 <- read_feather("tmp2.feather")
  final_df <- bind_rows(featherdf1, featherdf2)
})
````
This doesn't work, but might be how this could go:
```
pryr::mem_change({
  feather1 <- feather("tmp1.feather")
  feather2 <- feather("tmp2.feather")
  final_df <- bind_rows(feather1, feather2) %>% collect()
})
file.remove("tmp1.feather", "tmp2.feather")
```

title: Date class from R -> Python -> R is not retained
description:
When writing a `tibble` with a `Date` column from `R -> feather -> Pandas -> feather -> R`, the `Date` class is lost and becomes `POSIXct`. 

I think this is happening when the python version of `feather` reads the file and converts it to a pandas DataFrame. It brings in the date column as `datetime64[ns]` which is then resaved as `datetime`, not `date`. But I am not sure if this is actually where the problem lies.

Using `reticulate` in R, here is a full reproducible example.

``` r
library(reticulate)
library(feather)
library(tibble)

PY_FEATHER <- import("feather")

tf <- tempfile(fileext = "feather")
tf2 <- tempfile(fileext = "feather")

ex <- tibble(date_col = as.Date("2018-01-01"))
ex
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   date_col  
#>   <date>    
#> 1 2018-01-01

feather::write_feather(ex, tf)

# No problem here
feather::read_feather(tf)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   date_col  
#>   <date>    
#> 1 2018-01-01

# Metadata is "date". This is correct.
feather::feather_metadata(tf)
#> <Feather file>
#> [1 x 1] @ /var/folders/ln/vjgktwwx50jcvm7jq7jlnsbr0000gn/T//Rtmp3en49k/file13e6755c571eefeather
#> * 'date_col': date

# Now read into pandas
ex_pd <- PY_FEATHER$read_dataframe(tf)

ex_pd
#>     date_col
#> 0 2018-01-01

# And write it back using feather
PY_FEATHER$write_dataframe(ex_pd, tf2)

# Now read it back into R - Lost date, now reading as datetime
feather::read_feather(tf2)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   date_col           
#>   <dttm>             
#> 1 2017-12-31 19:00:00

# The metadata is written incorrectly as datetime
feather::feather_metadata(tf2)
#> <Feather file>
#> [1 x 1] @ /var/folders/ln/vjgktwwx50jcvm7jq7jlnsbr0000gn/T//Rtmp3en49k/file13e6715baec40feather
#> * 'date_col': datetime
```

title: read_feather method does not restore a dataframe's table-level user-defined properties (attributes or tags or metadata)
description:
I create a property named _someid_ (it is NOT a column) in a pandas dataframe named _df_ and assign it a value:
`df.someid = 24`
I make sure the property is there:
`print(df.someid)  #prints 24`
I save the dataframe to a feather file:
`df.to_feather("C:/pandas/DataLoss.feather")`
I read the feather file back into a dataframe:
`df = pd.read_feather("C:/pandas/DataLoss.feather")`
I try to retrieve the property from the dataframe:
`print(df.someid)  `
And I do not get its value (24) back.  Instead I get this error message:
```
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AttributeError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-99-42d4540986ab> in <module>()
----> 1 print(df.someid)

~\Anaconda3\envs\env_feather\lib\site-packages\pandas\core\generic.py in __getattr__(self, name)
   3079             if name in self._info_axis:
   3080                 return self[name]
-> 3081             return object.__getattribute__(self, name)
   3082 
   3083     def __setattr__(self, name, value):

AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'someid'
```

1.  This may well be by design, although afaik undocumented, but it seems to me that an error should be generated whenever user data is lost--if the feather format is intended to be the native storage format for a pandas dataframe.  (However, the inability to store indexes is documented; fwiw, I wish that limitation weren't present either.)
2.  Or it may be there is a newer, better way of specifying user properties (tags / metadata) that I don't know about, in which case perhaps the old method should give a warning and be deprecated.
3.  Note that I could store the property as a column (as a repeating constant), but that uses up significant space as the number of rows increases (as the value repeats on every row)--even if stored as a categorical.  That wouldn't be an issue if there were compression, but there appears not to be compression.  I could use parquet format instead, and perhaps in the latest release that would be recommended over feather format.  (I haven't seen a good comparison of the pros and cons of each.)

Thanks for any assistance or comments.  (--Apologies in advance if I missed something in the docs or online; I didn't see anything relevant after a reasonable search, except the unapproved use of the undocumented __metadata_.)  

I realize there are thorny, perhaps unresolvable, problems with dataframe table-level metadata propagation (e.g. how to handle vertical dataframe concatenations), but I think what happens (by design) should be documented.  As it is, I don't know what is supposed to be happening by design here.

title: Feather current state / future?
description:
Wes, feel free to point me somewhere else if this is the wrong forum for this. I'm intrigued with Feather and Arrow and am curious as to where things stand right now. Particularly in light of these comments:

> As time has passed, as one might expect, quite a bit of code overlap has developed between Feather's C++ and Python components and Apache Arrow's respective C++ and Python libraries. To address this, I'm planning to merge the Feather implementation into the Arrow codebase, which will enable me to provide better performance and new features to Feather users. ([Source](http://wesmckinney.com/blog/outlook-for-2017/).)

> Feather is not designed for long-term data storage. At this time, we do not guarantee that the file format will be stable across versions. Instead, use Feather for quickly exchanging data between Python and R code, or for short-term storage of data frames as part of some analysis. ([Source](https://blog.cloudera.com/blog/2016/03/feather-a-fast-on-disk-format-for-data-frames-for-r-and-python-powered-by-apache-arrow/).)

I'm transitioning to Python / Pandas (from SAS and Stata) and really like the performance and interoperability aspects of Arrow and Feather. Is it still too early for me to rely on either for long-term storage? Also, it sounds like Feather is being deprecated. If I'm just getting started with both, should I be focused on Arrow?

Appreciate your thoughts as well as everything you've put into developing this!

title: Creating feather files from data stream with small memory footprint
description:
Hello,

This is very similary to issue #272, but for writing feather files.

I am planning to use arrow's C++ API (installed in `arrow/ipc/api.h`) to create **feather** files so I can rapidly read them in R to ingest data in my tidyverse code. So, as of now, the only way to do it is to keep all columns in memory (using `arrow::DoubleBuilder->Append` for each column as objects in the data stream arrive) and at the end, when the stream finishes, call `feather_table->Append` with the name of each column and the corresponding in-memory array of values. The problem is that my input is a stream, and I want to avoid keep it all in memory. So, in a hypothetical ideal scenario, I'd create one table row at a time (eventually buffering multiple rows for performance reasons) and do a "row bind" operation in feather's TableWriter periodically. Such scenario, as far as I known, is impossible with the current arrow's feather C++ API since it let me manage only finished columns.

An `R` alternative would be to call `read_csv` (from the `readr` package) once the stream is finished, and them `write_feather` to get the appropriate feather files; but I want to avoid CSV files. Despite being slow on scale (> 100M lines with ~20 columns each), the costly parsing procedure creates a lot of temporary objects in memory.

What would be the best way, if possible, to do this with feather files? Thanks.

title: Later optimizations: designing for IO/CPU pipelining
description:
Reading a table from a file will consist of two steps for each column:
1. Read/decompress appropriate bytes from file
2. Convert bytes to native representation in Python/R/other target

So when reading a table with N columns, each of these steps occurs N times. Without a complete library hard to estimate what % of time is spent in each step, but we'll want to pipeline the steps so that the file reader/decompressor and move onto paging the next column into RAM while the previous one is being converted to its Python/R destination data structure. The pipeline can throttle itself based on the total amount of unprocessed memory allocated.

title: Question: Feather very slow when reading file for the first time
description:
I've noticed that on Windows (haven't tested Linux) reading in a file with Feather is very slow the first time, but after that it's very fast.

I've noticed times of almost a minute at worst, with subsequent reads being about 3-4 seconds (this is a 1.8GB file). Using an SSD or HDD doesn't seem to result in much a difference.
The same behaviour seemed consistent between R and Python.

Is this by design, or am I doing something wrong?

title: decouple from tibble - support R-3.1.1
description:
Apologies if this is the wrong forum for this comment.

Feather has been a godsend for me and would be ubiquitous in my work, however its coupling with tibble prevents that. The issue isn't with tibble per se - though tibble seems like sugar and is unrelated to feather's core concern. However, tibble only supports >= R-3.1.2 and for legacy reasons I'm locked into R-3.1.1.

Feather itself doesn't require R-3.1.2 and I don't see anything in the 3.1.2 [changelog](https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-announce/2014/000578.html) that seems relevant. As far as I can tell, excising the tibble imports and tibble::as_data_frame everything would still just work.

Is it feasible to suggest tibble and not lock out those stuck with R-3.1.1?

title: Feather IO subsystem behaves improperly when the user attempts to overwrite an existing file
description:
Files are not being truncated to 0 bytes before being written if they already exist -- this will cause corrupted metadata in a lot of cases if the data written is smaller than the original file (because the writes still happen from the beginning of the file).

There are already a lot of bug reports (#248, ...) that are caused by this problem. We should fix and make a bugfix release as soon as practical

title: Issues with pandas.SparseDataFrame
description:
I just ran into some issues with feather and sparse pandas DataFrames (Python 3.5). `feather.write_dataframe()` doesn't raise exceptions but `feather.read_dataframe()` might drop values (both v0.2 and v0.3) or raise a ValueError (v0.2) / a FeatherError (v0.3):

```
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import feather
>>> import numpy as np
>>> df = pd.DataFrame([[0,np.nan],[np.nan,1]]).to_sparse()
>>> df.info()
<class 'pandas.sparse.frame.SparseDataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 2 entries, 0 to 1
Data columns (total 2 columns):
0    1 non-null float64
1    1 non-null float64
dtypes: float64(2)
memory usage: 96.0 bytes
>>> df
     0    1
0  0.0  NaN
1  NaN  1.0
>>> feather.write_dataframe(df, 'test.feather')
>>> df2 = feather.read_dataframe('test.feather')
>>> df2
     0    1
0  0.0  1.0
```

The NaN values were dropped and row 0 and 1 merged into one row.

```
>>> df = pd.DataFrame([[0,1],[1,1]]).to_sparse(fill_value=1)
>>> df
     0    1
0  0.0  1.0
1  1.0  1.0
>>> feather.write_dataframe(df, 'test.feather')
>>> df2 = feather.read_dataframe('test.feather')
```

at this point v0.2 raises a ValueError:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/.../site-packages/feather/api.py", line 61, in read_dataframe
    return pd.DataFrame(data, columns=names)
  File "/.../site-packages/pandas/core/frame.py", line 224, in __init__
    mgr = self._init_dict(data, index, columns, dtype=dtype)
  File "/.../site-packages/pandas/core/frame.py", line 318, in _init_dict
    extract_index(list(data.values()))
  File "/.../site-packages/pandas/core/frame.py", line 5279, in extract_index
    raise ValueError('arrays must all be same length')
ValueError: arrays must all be same length
```

while v0.3 raises a FeatherError instead:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/.../site-packages/feather/api.py", line 58, in read_dataframe
    reader = ext.FeatherReader(path)
  File "feather/ext.pyx", line 214, in feather.ext.FeatherReader.__cinit__ (feather/ext.cpp:3704)
  File "feather/ext.pyx", line 55, in feather.ext.check_status (feather/ext.cpp:1666)
feather.ext.FeatherError: Invalid: File is smaller than indicated metadata size
```

Are sparse structures generally incompatible with feather-format? If so, maybe there should be at least a warning on feather.write_dataframe(), when a SparseDataFrame is provided. Or is it possible/sensible to make this work?

BR,
Jonathan

I am collecting a list of tweets and them mapping them to a data frame with code that looks like this: ``` python import glob import pandas as pd import json import feather def get_body(tweet): body = tweet.get('body') if body == None: return 'NA' return body def get_datetime (tweet): datetime = tweet.get('postedTime') if datetime == None: return 'NA' return datetime def get_location(tweet): actor = tweet.get('actor') if actor == None: return 'NA' location = actor.get('location') if location == None: return 'NA' display_name = location.get('displayName') if display_name == None: return 'NA' return display_name input_folder = 'SandyHook/SH8/*.json' output_file = './tweets_df/sh8.feather' tweets_data =[] file_count = 0 for file in glob.iglob(input_folder, recursive=True): tweets_file = open(file, "r") file_count = file_count + 1 if file_count % 50 == 0: print('file count is ' + str(file_count)) for line in tweets_file: try: if 'body' in line: tweet = json.loads(line) tweets_data.append(tweet) except: continue df = pd.DataFrame() df['tweet'] = [get_body(tweet) for tweet in tweets_data] df['datetime'] = [get_datetime(tweet) for tweet in tweets_data] df ['location'] = [get_location(tweet) for tweet in tweets_data] feather.write_dataframe(df, output_file) ``` When I read some of the feather data frames into R, the first column gets overwritten with the second column (inconsistently) -- or a couple of times the last column gets transformed to TRUE/FALSE. title: Avoid memset with NULL ptr for 0 bytes
description:
One of the problems as raised by ASAN in https://github.com/wesm/feather/issues/163 for data frames appears for data frames with 0 rows. 

The problem is that **`memset()` may never be called `ptr = NULL` even when `num == 0`**. This problem appears several times in [feather-write.cpp](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/R/src/feather-write.cpp#L11-L19) when `nbytes = 0` for example:

``` cpp
auto buffer = std::make_shared<OwnedMutableBuffer>();
stopOnFailure(buffer->Resize(nbytes));
memset(buffer->mutable_data(), 0, nbytes);
```

The same problem appears later again when `AppendPrimitive` gets called with a null pointer for the `&values` parameter, which is not allowed.  

There are two possible solutions:
1. condition each call to `memset` on `if(nbytes > 0)` and change `&values` to `*values`
2. make `OwnedMutableBuffer` return a dummy pointer for `buffer->Resize(0)`

I think the latter would be more correct.

title: Add an "epoch" field to TimestampMetadata/DateMetadata?
description:
Some systems use epoch's different from 1970-01-01, such as 0000-01-01 (Rata Die epoch), or Julian epoch (-4713-11-24T12:00:00).

I wonder if it would make sense to add an `epoch` string field to the TimestampMetadata and DateMetadata types in order to capture the epoch of the time values in those columns.

I realize there's always a tradeoff between allowing more functionality and keeping things simple, but it would, for example, greatly simplify the Julia DateTime conversions (which are based on the Rata Die epoch due to the simplicity of different date calculations it allows).

description: I'm working on a feather writer for Julia and noticed a peculiarity while trying to match byte-for-byte a feather file I generated from pandas/python. As I was digging into byte differences between my generated file and the pandas-generated file, I noticed that the pandas-generated file has the feather magic bytes `FEA1` after each primitive double array. Is this actually part of the spec? I tried digging around source and couldn't even find where those bytes are being written. I can provide a more concrete example if needed, but just wanted to throw it out there in case there's an easy response.

title: feather.read_dataframe does not read in columns in correct order
description:
Hello,

First off I love the package, especially because I frequently pass data between Python and R.

I found what may be a bug where a dataframe exported from R doesn't have the same column ordering when read into Python, instead it appears that the columns are sorted in alphabetical order. When exporting and then importing a dataframe in R, the column order is preserved. 

**To reproduce the issue:**

feather-test.R

``` R
library("feather")
library("dplyr")

write_columns <- function(data, path) {

    # Writes the columns of a data.frame to text to use in conjunction with
    # feather for passing data in between Python and R
    data_frame(Names = names(data)) %>%
        write.table(path, row.names = FALSE, sep = '\t')
}

# Writing iris
iris <- as_data_frame(iris)
names(iris) <- gsub("\\.", "_", names(iris))
write_feather(iris, "iris.feather")

# Reading iris
iris_read <- read_feather("iris.feather")
print("Correct column order using read_feather")
print(identical(names(iris), names(iris_read)))

# Writing iris's column names
write_columns(iris, 'iris-columns.txt')
```

feather-test.py

``` python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import feather


def read_feather(myfile, columns):
    """
    Reads a feathered file into a Pandas DataFrame, using a .txt file of column 
    names to place columns in the correct order.
    """
    data = feather.read_dataframe(myfile)
    cols = pd.read_csv(columns, sep = '\t')
    return data.ix[:, list(cols['Names'])]


def correct_colorder(DataFrame):
    correct = ['Sepal_Length', 'Sepal_Width', 'Petal_Length', 'Petal_Width', 
               'Species']
    return list(DataFrame) == correct


iris = feather.read_dataframe('iris.feather')

print 'Correct column order for feather.read_dataframe?', correct_colorder(iris)

iris2 = read_feather('iris.feather', 'iris-columns.txt')

print 'Correct column order for read_feather?', correct_colorder(iris2)
```

Run

``` bash
Rscript feather-test.R
python feather-test.py
```

I am using Ubuntu 14.04 LTS with Python 2.7 and R 3.3.0. You can see my makeshift solution here where in R I use a `write_columns` function to write out the column names in order of a dataframe, and then use the `read_feather` function in Python to read in the dataframe in lieu of `feather.read_dataframe`.

Thanks!

title: Question regarding 'memory specification' vs 'file format'.
description:
hi,

i was just trying to get my head around arrow, and was a bit puzzled by these two statements, which appear to be contradictory.

> Feather uses the Apache Arrow columnar memory specification to represent binary data on disk.

and:

> Because Arrow does not provide a file format, Feather defines its own schemas and metadata for on-disk representation.

Apache arrow _is_ a memory specification for representing binary data on disk, but at the same time does not provide a file format?

thanks

title: [feature request] can read_feather in R use skip?

I have a feature request for R's read_feather to be able to use the "skip" parameter found in read.csv. Normally when I write data to disk I also write comments for myself for how the data was generated and place them into the csv file. When reading this data back into R later on I use read.csv(..., skip = X). Will I be able to do the same with feather?

The resulting csv I would write would look like

```
#Note to self, this file came from ...
<<normal csv header>>
<<normal csv row>>
```

description:
I am trying to build feather on Windows7 64bit using R-patched (3.2.4) and Rtools 3.3.0 V1959 (as discussed in https://github.com/wesm/feather/issues/58). I sort-of followed @wesm's advice by cloning the repository and manually taking the actions in the [R/configure](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/R/configure). The build proceeds until [io.cc](https://github.com/wesm/feather/blob/master/cpp/src/feather/io.cc) whereupon it fails as Windows installations of gcc do not have sys/mann.h

The older answers (like in SO) which directed one to https://code.google.com/archive/p/mman-win32/ are not useful as that is a dead link now. Can anything be done to get around this?

Thank you.

title: Document the file format
description:
I'll add a markdown document for this, basically:

```
<4-byte magic number "FEA1">
<primitive array 0>
<primitive array 1>
...
<primitive array n>
<metadata>
<int32: metadata size>
<4-byte magic number "FEA1">
```

title: Hide flatbuffers dependency from users of `libfeather`
description: Since we will statically-link all of libfeather's dependencies (i.e. `libflatbuffers.a`), C++ users linking to libfeather should not have to include Flatbuffers in their build toolchain to use the library

title: Error handling
description:
On contemplation I'm thinking we should adopt `Status` objects and forbid C++ exceptions. This is such a small library that exceptions only serve to complicate bindings in other languages. I can handle them in Python but it's very annoying. It would make an ANSI C API for libfeather harder to build also. 

Doesn't have to get sorted this moment but just a thought

title: Implement the FileOutputStream
description: Haven't done this yet -- #23 only reads and writes data to/from in-memory buffers (which is perfectly fine for getting this thing off the ground).

title: How to store boolean data?
description: NumPy stores booleans in `uint8_t`, I expect R is the same. Should we do that for feather? The Arrow spec doesn't indicate a storage class for boolean data (Parquet for example does encode booleans in bits).
